entry.title: [BIP Draft] Co-signer Spending Policies
entry.summary:
A critical examination of the proposed policy format is needed before any code is written, ensuring that only robust elements persist and become shared assets rather than proprietary constructs. The primary consideration centers on whether policy itself is the appropriate abstraction for standardization or if attention should be directed elsewhere. Assessments are sought regarding potential shortcomings in the design, ambiguities, and scenarios where differing interpretations among co-signers could arise.
Several pivotal decisions remain unresolved and invite broad input. These include choosing between JSON or TLV encoding, determining whether an escape hatch feature must always be subject to a timelock, considering whether the statement format should instead be incorporated into the Discreet Log Contracts (DLC) specifications, evaluating the complexity and scope of the output expression language, and establishing the right moment to define blinded and enclave operational modes.
The initiative deliberately refrains from seeking formal recognition such as a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) number, endorsements, or immediate adoption. Instead, it remains an open discussion draft to encourage inclusive participation and critique.
To avoid becoming another closed, proprietary policy format, the project is developed transparently under the MIT license and shared publicly through platforms like bitcoindev, Delving, and GitHub prior to any implementation. The focus lies in standardizing the policy layer itself—distinct from any specific product—so that integration is possible across wallets, co-signers, oracles, and varied application domains such as lending. Building upon established standards including Taproot, Miniscript, descriptors, PSBTs, MuSig2, and DLC oracles ensures compatibility while introducing no new consensus protocols or oracle networks.
Ownership is intentionally distributed where appropriate. For example, the statement format is offered to DLC specification maintainers rather than retained privately. The policy format is designed to be testable, providing precise test vectors and clearly defining invalid inputs, which enables independent verification of compatibility without reliance on a single implementation.
True success is measured by achieving consensus across at least two independent implementations, both consistently generating identical policy identifiers and matching accept-or-reject outcomes for given documents. Until this level of interoperability is realized, the format does not qualify as a standard. The work acknowledges foundational contributions from figures such as Towns, Halseth, Rubin, and references BIP 89, aiming to unify various existing approaches rather than compete with them.
Active engagement with established ecosystem participants—including projects like Liquidium, Lendasat, Casa, Unchained, and Nunchuk—is encouraged to solicit feedback and gauge practical requirements for adoption, avoiding assumptions about their willingness to integrate the standard.
